title: The recipe nobody asked you to change
hook: Pepsi keeps winning the taste test. Do you change the world's most famous recipe?

profit.label: Sales
profit.hint: How much cola you sell today

future.label: Loyalty
future.hint: How much your fans love and trust Coke

intro.text: Atlanta, USA, 1984. You run Coca-Cola, the best-known drink in the world, made almost the same way for nearly 100 years. Coke still sells more than Pepsi, but for 15 years in a row it has been ahead by a little less each year, and your board wants you to stop the fall.

s_challenge.text: Since 1975, Pepsi has run the Pepsi Challenge in shops and markets. People sip two colas without seeing the names, and more of them pick Pepsi. When your own team runs the same kind of test, it gets the same answer: people prefer a sweeter taste.

d1.title: How to stop the fall
d1.setup: There is some good news: Diet Coke, launched in 1982, shows that new drinks can still win buyers. While making it, your lab also found a sweeter recipe that beat both Pepsi and your own Coke in tests.
d1.question: How do you stop the fall?
d1.advisor: Pepsi says the problem is our taste, and our own tests agree with them.

options.label: Turn the lab's sweeter recipe into a new Coke in secret. It may win, but it changes a 99-year-old drink.
options.outcome: You decide taste is the problem. A secret team works on a sweeter recipe, and in tests with nearly 200,000 people it beats both Pepsi and the old Coke.
options.why: Remember: sell what you stand for, not just specs. Taste is only a spec, a fact about the drink. Coke stood for a lifetime of habits and memories, and a secret new recipe got your team ready to change the thing fans loved most.
options.better: Keep the old recipe safe. Win with new drinks and fresh ads, the way Diet Coke did, and test new tastes as extra drinks.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you treated a fight about feelings as a fight about flavour.

options.label: Keep the recipe, and fight with new drinks and ads. Fans stay happy, but Pepsi keeps gaining for now.
options.outcome: You leave the recipe alone and put your money into new drinks and fresh ads. For a while Pepsi keeps gaining, and your board grows impatient. But your fans keep the taste they grew up with, and Diet Coke keeps winning new buyers.
options.why: Remember: sell what you stand for, not just specs. Taste was only one spec, a fact about the drink. Your name, your history and your fans' memories were worth more than a sip in a test.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you grew around your core product instead of changing it.

options.label: Cut prices so families get more Coke for their money. Sales may rise, but you earn less on every can.
options.outcome: Cheaper Coke wins back some buyers, until Pepsi cuts its prices too. Now both of you earn less on every can, and Coke is still falling behind.
options.why: Remember: sell what you stand for, not just specs. Price is a spec too, a number Pepsi could match in a week. A fight on prices also told your fans that Coke was worth less.
options.better: Protect your price. Give people new reasons to choose Coke, like new drinks and fresh ads.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you fought with discounts and made your own drink look cheap.

d2.title: The taste test winner

setup.text: The sweeter recipe has won your tests. But the tests measured taste, not how people would feel if their old Coke disappeared, and about 10 to 12 in every 100 testers said they were angry at the very idea of a change.

Your new drinks are selling, but Pepsi is still close behind, and your marketing team wants to use the lab's sweeter recipe. In early tests, a few people say they would be angry if the old Coke changed.

The fight on prices has left you with thin profits and no clear win, so your marketing team wants to use the lab's sweeter recipe. In early tests, a few people say they would be angry if the old Coke changed.

d2.question: What do you do with the new recipe?
d2.advisor: One Coke gives you one clear message, and the new taste wins the tests. But people have drunk the old one all their lives.

options.label: Sell the new taste as a second Coke. Fans keep the old one, but two Cokes may confuse buyers.
options.outcome: The sweet drink goes on shelves beside the old Coke. Pepsi gets no story about angry Coke fans, and your fans still have the drink they love.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. The new taste might win on the result, a nicer sip. The old Coke kept the feeling, so no fan lost anything.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you added a new choice instead of taking away an old one.

options.label: Replace the old Coke everywhere. One clear Coke, though fans lose the taste they know.

outcome.text: On April 23, 1985, at a big event in New York, you announce the first new recipe in 99 years, and the old one comes off the market. Pepsi celebrates: it gives its staff a day off and runs full-page newspaper ads.
You announce the new recipe and take the old Coke off the market. Pepsi celebrates with newspaper ads, and reporters start asking your fans how they feel.

options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. A sip test measures taste, not the feeling of a drink people grew up with. Your own research warned you that some fans would be angry.
options.better: Sell the new taste as an extra drink, or test it in a few cities first, and never take the old one away.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you took away what fans loved because a test said they would like something else.

options.label: Swap it in a few cities first. You learn more, but it's slower, and Pepsi will see it.
options.outcome: In a few test cities, the sweet drink takes the old Coke's place. Within weeks, those cities send you a pile of angry letters, and the newspapers soon hear about it.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Testing small sounded careful, but in those cities you took away the drink people had feelings for, and the anger was real.
options.better: Test the new taste without taking the old one away: sell it beside the old Coke.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you tested before going big, but still tested the wrong idea.

d3.title: The fans fight back

setup.text: By June about 1,500 fans call your phone line every day, and about 40,000 write letters. They form protest groups and buy up the old Coke. A survey says only 13 in 100 cola drinkers like the new taste: a sip in a test was one thing, but drinking it every day is another.
Within weeks, your phones are ringing all day and the letters won't stop. Fans form protest groups and buy up all the old Coke they can find.

d3.question: Your fans are furious. What do you do?
d3.advisor: If we back down, the world will say we failed. If we keep going, how many fans will we lose?

options.label: Spend big on ads for the new taste. Testers liked it, but angry fans may get angrier.
options.outcome: You pour money into ads for the new taste. A few people switch, but most fans feel you are not listening, and the protests get louder.
options.why: Remember: admit a mistake early and openly, then fix it. Ads can tell people about a product. They can't make people stop missing something they loved, and every week you defended it made fans feel you weren't listening.
options.better: Admit the mistake fast. Bring the old recipe back and say sorry.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you tried to out-shout your own customers.

options.label: Change the new recipe to taste more like the old one. You keep one Coke, but it takes months.
options.outcome: Your lab works all summer on a softer version of the new taste. But fans don't want a closer copy of their Coke. They want the real one back, and some switch to Pepsi for good.
options.why: Remember: admit a mistake early and openly, then fix it. Fans weren't asking for a better new taste. They wanted the old one back, and every month in the lab made them angrier.
options.better: Listen to what fans are asking for. Bring the old recipe back quickly and say sorry.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept fixing the new recipe when fans wanted the old drink back.

options.label: Bring back the old recipe and say sorry. Fans get it back, but the world sees you admit it.

outcome.text: On July 11, 1985, just 79 days after the change, you say sorry and bring back the old recipe, now called Coca-Cola Classic. TV news breaks into regular shows to report it, and your phone line gets 31,600 calls in two days.
Within weeks of the change, you say sorry and bring the old recipe back. The news spreads fast, and your phones fill with calls from happy fans.

options.why: Remember: admit a mistake early and openly, then fix it. Saying sorry is hard for a big company. You moved within weeks and gave fans back what they loved.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you admitted a big mistake fast and fixed it.

d3alt.title: What the buyers told you

setup.text: The sweet drink sits next to the old Coke. Sales show that some people like it, but most still reach for the taste they grew up with, and your sales team says two Cokes confuse shoppers.

In your test cities, many fans are angry that their old Coke is gone. In taste tests, people there still like the sweet drink, but they miss the old one. Your team is split on what that means for the rest of the country.

d3alt.question: What next for the sweet recipe?
d3alt.advisor: Most people who tried the new taste liked it. Isn't that a yes?

options.label: Put the new taste everywhere anyway. Most testers liked it, and one Coke is simpler.

outcome.text: Fans across the country get angry, just as your test cities warned. After a hard summer of protests, you give in and bring the old taste back.
When you take the old Coke off the shelves, fans across the country get angry. After a hard summer of protests, you give in and bring the old taste back.

options.why: Remember: test small first, and decide beforehand what result means yes. What your buyers did told you most still wanted the old Coke, and you went ahead anyway. A test helps only if you act on what it tells you.
options.better: Keep the old Coke as the star, and sell the sweet taste only as a side drink.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you ignored your own warning signs.

options.label: Sell it only in the towns where it sells best, though different Cokes cost more to run.
options.outcome: The sweet drink sells in a few places, but running different Cokes in different places is costly and confusing, and nobody is sure which Coke is the real one.
options.why: Remember: test small first, and decide beforehand what result means yes. "Some people liked it" was never a yes. Different Cokes in different towns split your effort for a small gain.
options.better: Make the old Coke the star everywhere, and keep the sweet taste as a clear side drink.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you played safe, but made your brand more confusing.

options.label: Keep the old Coke as the star, and keep the sweet one only as a small extra.

outcome.text: The old Coke goes back on the shelves in your test cities, with the sweet drink beside it. Fans calm down, and the sweet drink finds its own small group of buyers.
Fans keep the Coke they love, and the sweet drink finds its own small group of buyers. Slowly, your lead over Pepsi starts to grow again.

options.why: Remember: test small first, and decide beforehand what result means yes. The test said people liked the new taste but loved the old Coke. You acted on what it really said.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept your core safe and let the new idea earn its place.

text.text: Fans cheer, and Classic sells fast. You keep the new drink on sale too, so now two Cokes sit side by side in the shops: Classic, and the new, sweeter drink, which still carries the name Coca-Cola.
Fans cheer, and the old Coke sells fast again. You keep the new drink on sale too, so now two Cokes sit side by side.

Your lab works all summer, but the changed recipe wins few fans, and the protests won't stop. In the end you bring the old recipe back, but fans say you only listened when you had no choice. Now two Cokes share the shelf.
The ads cost a fortune and change few minds. Fans protest all summer, and in the end you bring the old recipe back. Now two Cokes share the shelf.
The old taste is back after a hard summer, and now two Cokes share the shelf. Many fans still haven't forgiven you.
In some towns shoppers find one Coke, and in others they find two. Your sales team wants one clear plan for the whole country.
The old Coke is still the star, and the sweet drink has a small group of fans. Pepsi is no longer gaining on you.

d4.title: Next year's ad money
d4.setup: Next year's ad money is fixed, and both drinks want it. The team behind the sweet drink asks for half. Whatever you back now will shape what people think Coke is.
d4.question: How do you split the ad money?
d4.advisor: Splitting it evenly is fair to both teams, and gives each drink a real chance.

options.label: Put nearly all of it behind the old Coke and let the sweet one fade, though its team will be upset.
options.outcome: You put your money behind the taste your fans chose, and the new drink quietly fades away. Shoppers know exactly which Coke is the real one.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Your fans had shown you which Coke gave them that feeling. You put your money there and stopped paying for a drink they didn't want.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you backed what your customers chose, not what you hoped they would choose.

options.label: Give each drink its own campaign, so each gets a fair chance, though each gets only part of the push.

outcome.text: You keep both drinks and give each its own ad campaign. Classic quickly sells more than the new drink, and within a few months it is again the best-selling regular cola, ahead of Pepsi. The new drink falls to about 3 in every 100 colas sold.
You split the money and give each drink its own ad campaign. The old taste sells far more than the new one, and half your ad money goes to a drink few people want.

options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Only one of your two Cokes gave fans the feeling they paid for, but you split your money and attention across both.
options.better: Put your weight behind the taste fans chose, and let the new drink fade quietly.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you split your effort between a winner and a loser.

options.label: Put most of it behind the sweet drink, since young people like their cola sweeter.
options.outcome: You back the new drink again. Fans feel ignored for a second time, and many of them decide Pepsi is the easier choice.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Young buyers liked the sweet taste, but your fans had told you twice which Coke gave them the feeling they wanted.
options.better: Back the drink your fans chose, and let the new one fade.
options.takeaway: In 1985 you kept pushing a product your customers had already rejected.

text.text: You never took your fans' favourite drink away. New drinks and fresh ads bring in new buyers, and Coke's lead over Pepsi grows again without a summer of anger.
You listened to what the test really said. The old Coke stays the star, the sweet drink stays a small extra, and Coke's lead over Pepsi grows again.
You made mistakes, but you listened quickly and backed the taste your fans loved. Coke ends the year stronger than Pepsi, and its fans know you will listen.

survivor.title: The comeback of the old Coke

text.text: By the end of 1985, Coca-Cola Classic is selling well ahead of both the new drink and Pepsi. The new drink is later renamed and dropped in 2002, and Coca-Cola comes out of it stronger.
The old Coke is back and selling again, but it took you a whole summer to listen. Coke stays ahead of Pepsi, and fans remember how long you made them wait.
You backed the wrong drink at the end, and some fans drift to Pepsi. Coke is still big and still ahead, but its lead is smaller than before the new drink.
You made some costly moves, but you listened in time. Your fans stay with you, and Coke stays ahead of Pepsi.

collapse.title: The cola that lost its fans

text.text: You pushed the new drink even after fans said no twice. Many of them switch to Pepsi for good, and the world's best-known drink loses its lead.
By the time you backed the taste your fans loved, too many of them had switched to Pepsi for good. The world's best-known drink loses its lead.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: Three costly calls are too many. The board has lost its trust in you, and it asks someone else to win the fans back.

realHistory: Coca-Cola was losing ground to Pepsi, which kept winning taste tests where people could not see the names. After tests with nearly 200,000 people, it replaced its 99-year-old recipe with a sweeter one on April 23, 1985. Fans were furious, and calls, letters and protest groups poured in. After 79 days, on July 11, 1985, the company said sorry and brought back the old recipe as Coca-Cola Classic. Within months Classic was again the top regular cola, ahead of Pepsi. The new drink fell to about 3% of the market and was dropped in 2002.
